title: Schleiermacher
hook: religion as the feeling of absolute dependence

segments.voice: Yesterday, Wesley's warmed heart: faith as a living trust you can feel, growing into holy love. Your line was heart and holiness. What did you notice in your heart? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-two.

A short experiment, no tools needed. Name one thing in this minute that you made yourself. The breath you just took? It came without asking. Your heartbeat? It started before you knew your own name. The floor under you, the light in the room, the language you're thinking in: all handed to you. Friedrich Schleiermacher, a German preacher and professor, pointed at that kind of givenness. He wrote a book for educated friends who thought religion was finished, a pile of old rules and stale arguments. He told them they were looking in the wrong place. Religion, he said, doesn't begin with rules or arguments. It begins deeper down, in a kind of feeling. Today, Schleiermacher.

In his book The Christian Faith, Schleiermacher tries to name the heart of religion in one phrase. In English it's usually given as the feeling of absolute dependence. Take it slowly. Feeling: not a mood like happy or sad, but an awareness underneath the moods, a sense of where you stand. Dependence: we know the partial kind all the time. You depend on the bus, on a paycheck, on a friend. And you push back on the world a little: you choose, you act, you change things. That's freedom, and it's real. But Schleiermacher says there's one relation where the push only goes one way. Your whole self, your freedom included, comes from somewhere you didn't make. That's absolute dependence. And the word God, for him, names the one we depend on in that way. The Bible has its own words for it. Paul, speaking in Athens, says of God: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being." A psalm pictures every creature waiting on God: "These wait all upon thee; that thou mayest give them their meat in due season." Schleiermacher had sharp critics. Some said he turned faith into a mood, moving the center from God speaking to humans feeling; Karl Barth, whom this path meets again soon, argued with him hard. His defenders answer that he meant something steadier than a mood: the plain fact of being held, finally noticed. Christians still argue about where he leads. But his question stays a fair one: before any argument, what is it like to be a creature?
screen: `FAITH BEGINS IN FEELING` · `PARTIAL AND ABSOLUTE DEPENDENCE` · `IN HIM WE LIVE, AND MOVE` · `A MOOD, OR A FACT?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel your dependence. Settle, and breathe. Notice what's holding you right now. The chair or the floor under you. The air coming in without being asked. Your heart, keeping time on its own. Then go a little wider: the people who grew the food you ate today, the ones who taught you to read, whoever first said your name. Let the list run on past what you can name. You don't have to call it anything. If you pray, you can rest in Paul's line: in him we live, and move, and have our being. The bell holds the time.
Schleiermacher. The German theologian who said religion begins in a feeling: the sense of being utterly dependent, a whole life received.
Your line: entirely held. Today, at one meal, before the first bite, name three hands that brought it to you, from the field to your plate. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Christians who draw on Schleiermacher often describe prayer less as asking and more as resting in awareness of God as the source of all things; his thought is studied in Protestant seminaries and debated across the churches.
